speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MONTREAL RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called I should like to put this question to the Minister of Labour: Has anything been done to help the city of Montreal in matters of relief, pending the checking up of the accounts of the city by the provincial officials?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour) :
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
subtopic: MONTREAL RELIEF ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the position of the city of Montreal has upon a number of occasions

been the subject of some interrogations in this house. I have tried to make it clear that with respect to direct relief and other matters the province of Quebec is functioning under an agreement couched in the same terms as the agreement which prevails with the province of Ontario. During the past year, and particularly in the year 1933, great difficulty seems to have been encountered by the province of Quebec in rendering account to the dominion in order that the share of the dominion under the agreement could be promptly transmitted to the province of Quebec for payment to the city of Montreal. Just what the difficulties are I am not fully prepared to state, but the fact is that the dominion has not been receiving accounts from the province of Quebec.
Undoubtedly one of the difficulties is that the city of Montreal and the auditors of the province of Quebec have not been able to settle upon the proper amounts that are payable to the city of Montreal. The question has become acute, and for some time past this government has had under consideration some method which might be adopted in order to assist the city out of its present troubles. The province of Quebec as late as November last was urged to try to have its accounts submitted to Ottawa without the undue delay which had been experienced for many months prior to that date. But very little headway seems to have been made. The government, therefore, acting through myself, has to-day caused a message to be dispatched to the premier of the province of Quebec, reading as follows:
By reason of the prolonged delay which has occurred in respect of the completion by your provincial officials of the audit of the city of Montreal's relief accounts, and the acute financial difficulties which that city is experiencing by reason of the consequent nonpayment of the dominion and provincial proportions of the same, the dominion on the assumption that there will be approximately $3,000,000 payable by the dominion and an equal amount by the province, under the terms of the agreement, is prepared to make an accountable advance to the province of Quebec of $3,000,000 which with an equal amount from the province in respect of its share would provide the city of Montreal with $0,000,000, and greatly improve its present financial position. The proposed advance by the dominion would be made on the same terms as similar advances have been made to other provinces for similar purposes. At the same time I would again stress the importance of the provincial audit of Montreal's accounts

Bank Act
being carried out with all possible expedition in order that a financial adjustment of the dominion's accountable advance above referred to can be made with the least possible delay.

Mr. Chairman, I have consulted the Department of Justice with respect to this proposed amendment which was moved by my hon. friend in the committee on banking and commerce, and while I have not a final opinion from them they raise the question as to whether it is really competent in a matter having to do with banking to go beyond the bank and attempt to provide by way of legislation with respect to other creditors, having in mind the fact that the question has a bearing upon property and civil rights, which is a matter under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. For that reason alone I feel that it would be unwise to place an amendment in the act which might prove of no avail.
I might point out further that the difficulty which my hon. friend has in mind in moving his amendment has not arisen in practice to any appreciable extent. The section in question has been in force for some fifty years. There was some question bearing upon this point which arose in the decision af the case of the Victor Varnish Company, in re Clare's claim, reported in 16 Ontario law reports, 1908, but that is some twenty-six years ago. Notwithstanding that decision there has not been any demand made upon the department nor any suggestion offered, except that made by the hon. member for Cariboo, that the section should be amended. Under all the circumstances I feel that the amendment should not be entertained.

I sympathize entirely

It seems to me that there is no good reason why a man who guarantees a note to the bank should not be placed in the same position as the bank with regard to security when he pays that note. Of course, we must bow to the opinion of the Department of Justice with regard to the constitutionality of such a provision but I think there is a great deal of room for argument that it is part of a genuine banking bill to provide that guarantors of

obligations to banks, which are incidental to banking business, should have certain rights with respect to the security which the bank holds. It seems to me that this is a distinct improvement in our banking legislation and will facilitate banking. It will make a man a little more ready to assist his neighbour or his partner in connection with obligations if he knows that he will be subrogated to the rights of the bank in connection with the securities which the bank holds. I wonder if the minister feels that he should not go further with this matter and pursue his inquiry as to the constitutionality of the section, especially when he has no objection to the amendment on its merits.

They will not even put themselves out to send a second notice to the man who really got the money but they will go after the endorser who has no recourse but to pay. The. subsection states that there shall be no charge unless by express agreement between the 'bank and the customer but I understand the banks take the position that they are entitled to make such a charge when a man signs for his cheques at the end of the month and certifies that the account is correct. Bank Act

whether it is considered sufficient for the bank merely to make a charge, and because the customer accepts his account as correct, as stated, whether that binds him without an express agreement? Do the words express agreement require any obligation in writing?

With all deference, there is in my judgment nothing in the point that the individual has no alternative inasmuch as there may be only one bank in the community and therefore no opportunity for him to go elsewhere, having in mind the fact that the charge itself might and probably would be a reasonable charge, or rather that the principle of charging would be reasonable. This matter was inquired into by the Royal Commission on Banking and Currency and is referred to in paragraph 257 at page 74 of their report. They state:
The reasonableness of the banks making by agreement charges for services rendered in administering active accounts, when the customer offers no collateral or compensating advantage to the bank, has been recognized by the Bank Act, and rightly so. Any other mode of procedure would result in the shifting of the costs of performing certain services from one class of customers to another class.
I have only to add, with respect to the further query of my hon. friend, my belief that in practice the customer always signs a printed document which constitutes the agreement.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN TEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS

With regard to these service charges I have only one or two observations to make after listening to what the bankers themselves have had to say in this respect. These charges, in practice, are not nearly so innocent as they look when you are discussing the matter in the way we are. I only want to bring to the attention of the committee a case that came to my notice when I was travelling around the country and coming in contact with men whom I scarcely knew. I could cite a dozen instances, but the most striking example I submit now to show what is the actual practice in connection with these charges. This man lived in an outlying community and he told me he had been in the habit of carrying balances for months before the time of the occurrence-balances anywhere from $3,000 to $5,000. He was a general merchant in an outlying community. On B certain day he knew he had a number of obligations coming due and cheques that would be presented-it was a mail day-and he was very busy in his store. He overlooked making the deposit until after three o'clock. He went to the bank after three o'clock with a sufficient deposit to more than take care

of the obligations he had, but the bank was closed, and the next day when he went to clear up the deposit the manager charged him fifty cents for taking care of an overdraft of seventy cents during that time. I submit that as an actual occurrence, and I am satisfied that this man was telling the truth.
I have no objection to a service charge that is reasonable, but I want the general managers of banks to understand the situation. In actual practice the conditions which, impliedly, they lay down to their branch managers, are not carried out; their instructions are adhered to altogether too strictly. I think it would be well therefore for the banks to take up this matter to see whether they cannot loosen up on their instructions or have managers who will not follow those instructions as definitely and consistently as they do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN TEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext: Assuming the facts-and I do not call them in question-to be exactly as stated by my hon. friend from Cariboo, it seems to me that the only inference to be drawn from them is, to put it mildly, that that bank is unfortunate in having a manager with bad judgment.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN TEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext: That is as far as I go. However, the fact that he has brought forward this rather exceptional case; the fact that the matter was discussed in the committee on banking and commerce; and the further fact that the attitude of mind with respect to instances of that character has been brought home to the management of the banks, leave every reason to hope that these instances will be few and far between. They do not arise of necessity out of the statute, because they represent merely the abuse and not the proper use of the statute.

speechtext:
One great difficulty in connection with this matter of charges by banks is that there does not seem to be very much uniformity in the practice carried out in different sections of Canada, and sometimes not very much uniformity within certain sections. The complaints are many and varied. Of course, we anticipate some complaints, but I do not think there is much use discussing the matter at any great length in this committee; we discussed it at some length in the banking committee. It is a very difficult matter to legislate upon, but in some instances charges have been quite exceptional, running to as high as $2.50 a

Bank Act
month for a comparatively small account. One case was brought to my attention where the charges amounted to $4.50 for one month, in the case, too, of a man who was discounting a great many notes. As I say, it is a matter which it is very difficult to legislate upon and I am rather of the opinion that the only way to deal with it satisfactorily is to set up some sort of tribunal to whom aggrieved persons may appeal if they think they are unfairly dealt with by the banks in regard to service charges. Many of these people live in communities where there is only one bank, and the banks are becoming more and more in the nature of public service institutions, so that before very long, in my opinion, some method will have to be devised of regulating service charges.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN TEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
Section 138, if carefully examined, will be admitted by many members to be very objectionable indeed. The effect of this section is that only banks can issue money or substitutes for money; more than that, it is only banks which are chartered by this act. This gives these banks the absolute monopoly of the issue of the medium of exchange. If people have goods and services to exchange and have no money and can get none from the banks, why fine them $400 if they can invent a substitute for money? That is something I cannot understand. Is not this section putting people in so far as the issue of money is concerned at the mercy of the banks? Clause 138 reads:
Every person, except a bank to which this act applies, who issues or reissues, makes, draws or endorses any bill, bond, note, cheque or other instrument, intended to circulate as money, or to be used as a substitute for money, for any amount whatsoever, shall incur a penalty of $400.
It seems to me that a cheque is either money or a substitute for money. Which is it? Any person other than a bank that issues a cheque is liable to a fine of $400. It is true that there is perhaps an exception under subclause 4 if the cheque is for less than $20 but even in such a case it is only when the cheque is payable directly to the creditor of the immediate issuer that it is not considered a substitute for money. If that cheque passes through the hands of a third or fourth person, then under the terms of subsection 4 it becomes a substitute for money and the issuer
is liable to a fine of $400. If the cheque is for more than S20, according to this section it is a substitute for money, it would be a contravention of the clause itself. It is money or a substitute and it is a contravention of this clause because it is not issued by the banks. The whole clause appears to me to be very objectionable and bad law.
I would also address this question to the minister: What about a cheque issued on a trust or loan company? There are thousands of these cheques issued every week. Are they money or substitutes for money? As I understand the matter, they must be either one or the other. Under this section there seems to be the possibility of endless litigation. It is bad legislation, apparently designed to give the banks the monopoly of the issuing of our medium of exchange.
Subclause 3 which provides for a moiety of the penalty to the informer is bad law and should have no place in this bill. It is a disgrace to parliament to pass subclause 3 which provides that a moiety of the penalty goes to any person who becomes an informer. That is bad enough when it is incorporated in the Customs or the Excise Act, but to put it into such a respectable measure as the Bank Act is beyond my imagination, and as I said before, it is a disgrace to parliament if we pass it.
Subclause 4 reads:
The intention to pass the same as money shall be presumed.
I would invite hon. gentlemen just to take a few minutes to study this subclause which reads:
If any such instrument is made for the payment of a less sum than $20, and is payable either in form or in fact to the bearer thereof, or at sight, or on demand, or at less than thirty days thereafter, or is overdue, or is in any way calculated or designed for circulation, or as a substitute for money, the intention to pass the same as money shall be presumed.
Surely that is bad law. It is contrary to the old English maxim that a man is innocent till he is found guilty. It says:
The intention to pass the same as money shall be presumed-
Then it goes on to say:
-unless such instrument is a cheque on some chartered bank paid by the maker directly to his immediate creditor.
Again I raise the point: What about this cheque when it goes into the hands of a third or fourth party? What if it is drawn on a loan or trust company? What if it is for more than $20? I think clause 138 should be deleted from this measure-and I hope I shall have the support of many hon. members in the committee-because there are certain
Bank Act

features which are so objectionable and I cannot see any necessity for their being in the Bank Act. If there is necessity for placing anywhere in the statutes of Canada the provision that no one but the banks should issue money, it should be in some other act than the Bank Act, which applies only to banks, and anything of this kind having to do with organizations other than banks should be stated in the criminal code or in the Currency or the Dominion Notes Act which deal with the particular business of issuing money. I appeal to the minister to allow the deletion of clause 138 from the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN TEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
My hon. friend will appreciate the fact that there must be some protection for a country's currency. It may be arguable whether it is good policy even from a national viewpoint that the privilege of issuing currency should be delegated to banks. I need not enter into that question for the very obvious reason that the Bank of Canada Act provides that ultimately the whole of the currency shall be issued by a quasinational institution, the Bank of Canada. Therefore in very large measure, whatever force there may be in the hon. member's argument, it falls to the ground for the reason it is in the interests of the state itself that it should preserve its currency inviolate.
As regards his reference to the provision with respect to cheques, he must bear in mind that the statute itself provides that it is only in those cases where such cheques are used as a substitute for money with the object of defeating the note circulation privilege that any of the penalties would apply.
I do not propose to enter into an argument with him as to the question of the provisions of subclause 3 of this clause. I may say to him very frankly it is a provision of the law that I do not like, but that is only my personal view. It does not follow that because that provision has been in the law for years and years it must therefore remain, but I may point out to the committee that the same provision is found in numerous other acts touching various services of government and if we are to be consistent we should not make fish of one and flesh of another. If parliament in its wisdom-and I would not quarrel with it-were to decide that that principle should be abandoned and disappear entirely from our legislation, I would be quite in accord but I do not know that we should centre our objections to it upon the Bank Act in particular. I have only this to say, that my information is that in the light of experience this subclause has not lent itself to abuse and so far as I am aware no

harm has been done to the public by reason of that provision having been in the Bank Act for a period of years.
There is, I know, in some quarters the opinion that there should be the right on the part of municipalities to issue scrip. There are no doubt instances where that privilege might be exercised with benefit to the particular community and with no detriment to the banking situation in the country, but if that policy were recognized as a general thing it would have a tremendously disturbing effect upon the country's currency and credit which, I say, should be entirely under the control of the central authority.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN TEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
I am glad the minister holds subclause 3 rather in, I suppose I might say, disrepute. As we are considering this whole section, I will suggest two amendments here which I would like to have considered separately. The first one deals with subsection (2). I move:
That section 138 be amended by striking out subsection (2) and substituting the following:-
Such penalty shall be recoverable with costs in any court of competent jurisdiction by the Attorney General of Canada.
The section now reads:
(2) Such penalty shall be recoverable with costs in any court of competent jurisdiction by any person who sues for the same.
It seems to me that if anyone is going to sue for this it should be the attorney general.

I wish only to say that
the proposed amendment should be considered in the light of the fact that there still remains in the section subsection (3). It would appear to me that my hon. friend should at least advise the committee that he proposes to move an amendment in connection with it.	[DOT]

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN TEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
If I may interrupt I will
state the amendment which I propose to move to subsection 3. The section now declares that:
A moiety of such penalty shall belong to the person suing for the same, and the other moiety to His Majesty for the public uses of Canada.
My objection to that section is the moiety belonging to the person who sues for the same. Under subsection 2 as it now stands there is of course an encouragement for someone to come and sue simply to get the moiety. I move:
That section 138 be amended by striking out subsection 3 and substituting the following:-
Such penalty shall belong to His Majesty for the public uses of Canada.

But we know in some other countries municipalities that have made very good use of the issuing of what is termed scrip have been prevented by the action of banks in their own country from carrying on the practice. The same thing may prevent municipalities in Canada from issuing anything at all in the nature of orders or warrants which would enable them to put some of their idle people to work and to carry out local improvements through the labour of those men. Anyone who reads clause 138 and particularly subclause 4 must admit it is very difficult for a municipality to decide whether anything it may issue of that nature will not be a contravention of the section. Seeing that we cannot have subclause 4 stricken out, it seems to me that there is nothing left to do but to move the amendment which I have. I must admit we have had some difficulty in deciding upon the proper wording so as not to make the amendment sound unreasonable or unacceptable or offensive to the government. a municipality should have the right to issue something of that nature. Clause 138 gives to the banks an absolute monopoly of issuing anything that is money or even a substitute for money. Some of these municipalities have plenty of goods and services to exchange but they have no money and can get none and if by issuing certain orders of their own they can have unemployed people put to work, collect back taxes and have local improvements done, I do not want to be a party to putting into this legislation something that will prevent them from doing so.
I do not wish to delay the committee but I would like to draw attention to what has been accomplished in certain municipalities. The best example I can give' at the moment is one the story of which is contained in a book by Professor Irving Fisher entitled Stamp Scrip. It relates to the experience of the Austrian town of Woergl where in 1931-32, 1,500 people had lost their jobs because a number of factories had closed their doors. The taxes, therefore, were in arrears, and the town itself was almost as down and out as these 1,500 of its inhabitants. The mayor of this town, I think a very shrewd man, adopted the idea of issuing stamp scrip. He had watched with very much interest a similar experiment in a smaller town and he arranged for the issue of a small amount of this stamp scrip. I am going to read only a paragraph or two at the end of the article. It says:
According to plan, on August 1, 1932, 32,000 schillings worth of the scrip (equivalent to about $4,500) was issued, in denominations of one, five and ten schillings.
This would amount to about one dollar per head of population.
This amount was later found to be in excess of the actual need, and instead of following an "inflationary policy," only about one-third of the issue or less was kept in circulation through reissues, the rest remained with the city.
These are the results. It says:
Soon everybody accepted it-
That is the scrip.
-without hesitation, because everybody else accepted it. The only cases of permanent refusal to receive the scrip are the post office and the railroad, both of which are government institutions with interests primarily outside of the vicinity where the scrip is supposed to circulate.
The attitude of the Austrian government has not been hostile.
As to the rate of turnover, the mayor reports that the amount of the first wages paid' has returned to the city twenty times a month.
The other facts are contained in a report which the mayor of Woergl made to the Tyrol state government, January 1, 1933.

During the first month alone, 4,542 schillings were thus received on the arrears. Accordingly, the city not only met its own obligations but. in the second half of 1932, executed new public works to the value of 100,000 schillings. Seven streets aggregating four miles were rebuilt and asphalted; twelve roads were improved; the sewer system was extended over two more streets; trees were planted and forests improved, and permanent jobs were given to from thirty to fifty of the 1,500 unemployed; but probably a powerful influence has been exerted to prevent any increase of unemployment, by keeping business active.

I do not think such action on their part should be considered a violation of clause 138; it is certainly not violating the purpose which clause 138 is intended to serve.

In times past rural municipalities could have their road work performed, and through a line of credit given them by a bank could issue a cheque in payment for it, the person performing the work could negotiate that cheque and with the proceeds buy his groceries and carry on. The road work is still to do and there are still people to do it, but many of our municipalities are not able to get a line of credit at

the bank. The road work should be done perhaps in the months of May and June, and the taxes for the payment of same are not available until .perhaps September or October. Those men have to buy their groceries, they have to have money to carry on current expenses. Under this proposal, as I understand it, it would be lawful for a municipality to issue a warrant, call it a day labour pay sheet or any other name you choose. The hardware man or grocer would hold the instrument until the fall and then turn it in to the municipality and secure the cash. As I understand that is what the amendment makes provision for. One can hardly understand why such a section as this should be found in the statutes of a modern civilized state. This subsection states:
Such officers, clerks and servants may be paid such salaries and allowances as the directors or such officer, in the case of appointments made by him, consider necessary.
During the last century we have come a long way from that position. This year in Great Britain they are celebrating the martyrdom of the Tolpuddle martyrs. These men are recognized throughout the civilized world as the fathers of the modern trade union movement. Because of a reduction in the very small wages paid at that time, these men formed what was to be a friendly society. They were tried, convicted and sentenced to transportation to Australia for seven years. Because of the agitation and the arousing of public opinion in Great Britain they were eventually pardoned and to-day five out of the seven now lie in churchyards around London, Ontario. This government adhered to the treaty of Versailles which contains certain labour sections which were drawn up under the guidance of a former Prime Minister of this country, Sir Robert Borden. At the present moment a committee is sitting in Geneva drawing up conventions for the guidance of the governments which are members of the League of Nations. Only yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) pointed out the contribution which the trade unions had made to the life of Canada and Great Britain. He referred to the forces which were arrayed against the working men and women in their efforts to establish what they considered to be civilized and social working conditions. In these late days we now have a section of a bill being passed by this parliament which gives to the bankers of this country complete control over the daily lives of

This bill gives enormous rights to the institutions in question and I think it is only fair that some right should be given to the employees. They should be permitted to organize if they so desire to bring about what they consider to be fair conditions of employment. They should be permitted to negotiate around a common table with their employers in order to establish conditions which they think are fair and equitable. It gives me great pleasure to move this amendment and I hope hon. members of the committee will realize its justness and soundness. In my opinion it is in conformity with present day thought and with the opinion expressed yesterday by the Prime Minister.
I am not going to go into details of the low wages paid by the banks to their employees as they are already on record. These wages are a disgrace to any civilized institution. They ask men from eighteen to twenty-three years of age to work for as low as $300 a year. Ledger-keepers from the ages of nineteen to forty-six years work for as low as $400 per year. Tellers from the ages of twenty-one to fifty-five years, receive S500 per year. Accountants from the ages of twenty-one to forty-nine years receive $700 a year. Managers of the ages from twenty-seven to sixty-four years receive $1,200. Women clerks and stenographers from seventeen to fifty years of age receive $300. I ask that this committee consider this amendment on its merits. I might point out in conclusion that the principle of allowing these employees to organize has been endorsed by the Trade and Labour Congress, the recognized mouthpiece of organized labour in this country, at many successive conventions.

Hon. ALFRED DURANLEAU (Minister of Marine) moved the second reading of Bill No. 91, intituled an act respecting shipping.
He said: In rising to say a few words on the second reading of this bill I think it is proper

Shipping Act-Mr. Duranleau
to give a brief history of the merchant ship^ ping laws as they affect Canada.
When confederation was formed in 1867 Canadian shipping was governed almost entirely by the merchant shipping laws or acts of the United Kingdom, because they were expressed to apply throughout the whole empire. It is true that the English laws contained provisions giving authority to the legislature of any British possession or any part of the empire to enact legislation repealing or modifying any provision of the British law relating to ships registered in Canada, and to regulate the coasting laws of those possessions. But it was provided that these enactments should not come into operation until approved and confirmed by Her Majesty, and that all British ships should receive the same treatment.
Shortly after confederation Canada commenced to enact merchant shipping legislation of her own under the authority granted by the British North America Act, section 91, subsection 10, Navigation and Shipping. I should like to refer to some of these earlier acts:
1.	Registration and classification of ships.
2.	Masters' and mates' certificates.
3.	Steamboat inspection, including engineers' certificates.
4.	Shipping of seamen.
5.	Shipping of seamen on inland water.
6.	Wrecks, casualties and salvage, etc.
When the revision of the Canadian statutes took place in 1906 the commissioners who were entrusted with that revision had to gather all these separate acts and put them into one act which they called the Canada Shipping Act; and from them the Canada Shipping Act was amended from time to time and now is chapter 186 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927; our present legislation.
The British merchant shipping act, as I said a moment ago, required that when the laws enacted by Canada or any other dominion were different from those contained in the imperial act, they had to be reserved until they were confirmed and approved by His Majesty the King. This situation remained until 1926 when at the imperial conference of that year representations were made as to the limitations contained in the British law, and it was resolved at that conference that an expert committee and subconference be set up to "study, to consider and report on the principles which should govern, in the general interest, the practice and legislation relating to merchant shipping, in the various parts of the empire having regard to the changes in constitutional status and general
legislation which have occurred since existing laws were enacted." This conference on the shipping laws met in London in 1929, and its recommendations were to the effect that the limiting provisions of the imperial statutes should be entirely wiped out. I am glad to say that this recommendation was given effect to in the statute of Westminster in 1931. Thus to-day, Mr. Speaker, for the first time Canada is entirely free to enact any legislation with regard to her shipping matters, and when necessary to give her legislation an extraterritorial effect without any reference to or without limitation by the imperial statutes. While the British merchant shipping acts were in effect in all dominions the result was, of course, a very great measure of uniformity. The different parts of the empire have thought it would be very wise to maintain as long as possible that uniformity. In 1931 the different parts of the empire came to an agreement which laid down the main lines along which legislation should be enacted in the different dominions. This convention is known as The British Commonwealth Merchant Shipping Agreement, and covers briefly: (1) common statutes in ownership, registration, etc., of British ships; (2) standards of safety; (3) extraterritorial operation of laws; (4) equal treatment; (5) ships articles, internal discipline, and engagement and discharge of seamen; (6) certificates of officers; (7) shipping inquiries; (8) relief and repatriation of seamen; wages and effects of deceased seamen; (9) offences on board ship, and (10) general provisions.
It was in the light of the statute of Westminster and the shipping agreement to which I referred a moment ago that the Department of Marine undertook in 1932 and in the first part of 1933 to formulate a shipping code which when enacted would give Canada full power over Canadian ships wherever they might be, and over all other British and foreign ships when they were within our territory. In the new code of shipping Which was drafted were incorporated the provisions of certain international conventions which were adopted in 1929 and 1930. I will refer particularly to two of those conventions to which almost all the nations of the world subscribed. I refer to the international convention for the safety of life at sea, which was adopted in 1929, and the international load line convention, which was adopted in 1930.
After engaging eminent counsel to assist them, the officers of the Department of Marine drafted a full revision of the Canada Shipping Act, following which a bill was presented to the Senate in 1933 by the Right Hon. Mr. 3S14

Shipping Act-Mr. Duranleau
Meighen which was known as bill J. This bill was referred by the Senate to its standing committee on banking and commerce where a study of the subject was begun. That committee called before it all those parties interested in shipping, namely the grain merchants, the ship owners, the shipbuilders, the pilots, the engineers, in addition to all those associations interested in shipping. When that discussion was in progress a point of law was raised and strong representations were made against certain provisions of the bill which purported to impose upon British consuls and other officials in other countries certain duties when, in fact, Canada has no jurisdiction over those officials. After a careful study of the point we came to the conclusion it had been well taken, and owing to the proximity of the end of the session in 1933 Bill J had to be withdrawn. It is interesting to note that when the bill J was under discussion in the Senate, copies of its text were circulated not only to the shipping interests in Canada but also to the chamber of shipping in London, England, and to the mercantile marine department of the Board of Trade, London; and we invited comments and representations from all those bodies both in Canada and abroad. Then, at the end of the year 1933 and in the early stages of this year, the officials of the Department of Marine, after having received all those representations, redrafted the bill under the direction of the Department of Justice, and it w*as reintroduced into the Senate. The bill was presented, on March 7 as Bill E, and was again sponsored by the right hon. leader of that body. It was referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce which in turn set up a subcommittee. The subcommittee, with the help of Mr. W. F. O'Connor, K.C., acting for the Senate, and Mr.. P. M. Anderson from the Department of Justice, made a careful study of the bill. May I add that this subcommittee sat throughout the Easter holidays and for some time following, during which time they made a very careful study of the legislation. The bill was amended in many respects in connection with important points, and as a result of the many changes made, it had to be reprinted for purposes of reporting to the full committee on banking and commerce. When that report was made the full committee heard again all the interested parties, the shipping associations, the ship owners, the shipbuilders, the labour associations and all those who wished to be heard. Following those hearings some further amendments were made, at the conclusion of which the bill was reported to the Senate and was adopted.
[Mr. Duranleau.1
I am pleased to state that after two months' study and discussion in the Senate the measure has been reported to this house in as complete form as possible. It comprises sixteen parts dealing with such varied matters as recording, registering and licensing; certificates of officers, masters and seamen, relief and repatriation of distressed seamen, sick mariners and marine hospitals, pilotage, safety, wrecks, salvage and investigation, lighthouses, buoys and beacons, harbours, harbour masters, port wardens, navigation, collisions, limitation of liability, coasting trade, delivery of goods, legal proceedings and so on.
This house will remember that when during the session of 1933, Bill J was withdrawn in the Senate a small bill was introduced in this house providing for certain amendments to the Canada Shipping Act respecting our coasting trade. That bill became law, and stood as chapter 52 of the statutes for 193233. May I add that the provisions of chapter 52 have been incorporated in the present bill.
I do not wish to close my remarks, Mr. Speaker, without paying tribute to the right hon. leader of the Senate, Mr. Meighen, and to the members of the Senate, and especially to the members of its standing committee on banking and commerce and the subcommitee for the tremendous work they have done in studying this measure. They had to spend weeks upon weeks in studying it, and so complete has their work been that they have rendered comparatively easy the task of this house in studying the measure. I am not an expert in maritime matters but I have perused and studied this bill with my officials and I can say that this measure is surely one of the most complete pieces of legislation ever presented to this house.

Mr. Speaker, at this particular time I am not going to raise any objection to the motion that this bill, letter E of the Senate, be now read a second time, but in the course of my remarks I shall give reasons why in my opinion it is impossible for the House of Commons at this late stage of the session to deal with this most important measure in a proper manner. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is necessary for me to say very much more on that point because the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) in the very instructive and able address which he gave in explaining this bill told us quite plainly that it is one of the most important bills that has ever been brought before this house.
The .minister in the course of his remarks went into the history of the various shipping

Shipping Act-Mr. Duff
acts in this country and the British Isles since confederation, and I was very glad indeed to hear him admit that Canada has authority to regulate her own shipping. That is one further reason why at this particular time we should not hurriedly go over this bill and pass most important clauses without knowing exactly what we are doing. It would be much more in the interests of Canada and in the interests of business and shipping, I submit, if we deferred consideration of this measure to a later date.
As I said a moment ago, I have no particular objection to the bill now being read the second time, nor, if it is the wish of the ministry, do I object to the bill being moved into committee after its second reading. But I do respectfully submit, Mr. Speaker, that in the interests of Canadian shipping after the bill has been moved into committee we should not endeavour to consider in detail this very important measure at this stage of the session, a measure about which most of us know so very little; but rather the minister should move that the committee rise and report progress, and at a later date, if not this session perhaps at another, we shall be in a position to deal intelligently rvith the bill.
I was very glad to hear the minister say that he and his officials had gone over this very important bill. That is more, sir, than I have been able to do.

I called it another place, Mr. Speaker, and the minister called it the Senate, so I think perhaps I should be allowed a little latitude. But of course I should know better, and perhaps that is the reason, sir, why you are calling me to order. There was no such suggestion on my part.

I am very glad, Mr. Speaker,
that we understand each other. I was saying that in another place this bill has been considered by a committee in two sessions, and this session that committee spent almost five months in considering it, with the result that it was only on Wednesday of this week that the members of the commons were able to get a copy of it. Again I am not complaining, because if you will look at this voluminous document you will see that the printers must have had quite a job to get it ready after it had been passed by the Senate. The fact remains that this bulky document was put into the hands of members of parliament only on Wednesday morning last. Taking the advice of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), tendered to me a few days ago, instead of going to the moving pictures on Wednesday night I spent from six o'clock until twelve, and the intervening time since then when I was not attending to my other duties, in reading some of the sections of the bill.
The house will see that this important document contains 497 pages, and not only are there 497 pages, but there are 113 definitions and 719 sections.
This afternoon we dealt with a very important measure in connection with banking and commerce,, and if I remember aright that bill contained about 170 sections. It took the members of the banking and commerce committee some two and a half months to study that bill and report upon it to the house. Surely then, Mr. Speaker, it is only fair for me to say that it would not be right or proper that a bill to which the minister himself attaches so much importance should proceed after its second reading on the eighth day of June, after being only two days in
Shipping Act-Mr. Duff

the hands of members of the House of Commons, to be considered in detail at this stage of the session.
In addition to the 497 pages, 113 definitions, and 719 sections, there are schedules in the bill extending from page 273 to 497; in other words, there are 224 pages of schedules alone. In order to make a thorough study of the bill it is necessary to compare each clause with the definition at the front of the bill. Then we must turn to the schedule pages to see exactly what effect the particular section will have on the schedules or the schedules upon the section. We are being asked to move into committee and endeavour to deal with this bill in a hurried manner. This bill is of vital importance to the shipping and business interests of this country .
The Minister of Marine stated that when this bill was before the Senate committee, both this year and last year, all interests connected with shipping had an opportunity to appear before that body. It is quite true that anyone who read the newspapers and saw that the bill was before that committee could come to this city and appear, but I [DOT]think my hon. friend will agree that no one came to Ottawa to appear before the committee who was interested either in the building or the owning of wooden ships. I was here during both years and no one paid me *the courtesy of asking me to give my limited knowledge and state what I thought about this bill. While the minister was right up to a certain point in stating that everyone had a chance to be heard-*

speechtext: I said everyone who wanted to be heard. I am sure that if my hon. friend had applied to the Senate he would have been heard.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) make the suggestion he has. I have no doubt it will meet with the approval of my hon. friend, the admiral of the fishing fleet of North America. I know it will meet with mine because I am taking a very deep interest in the passage of this bill. I should like to see its adoption deferred until next session, so that we might go very closely into all its provisions.
The Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) has told us that very great care was taken in the preparation of the bill, but I would point out to him that that care which in my opinion should have been taken has not been exercised. The greater shipping interest may have been attended to; but there are other interests in the shipping line which have not been considered at all in this bill. For instance, no regard has been had to the conditions of the fishing fleet on the Atlantic coast, and there are several reasons why particular attention should be given to that fleet in this bill. I do not wish to discuss any section of the bill; I am pointing this out simply to support the argument put forward by my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guys-borough (Mr. Duff) that the bill should go over for one year so that we might be in a position to go into it more thoroughly. To support that contention, let me point out that if this bill goes through as it stands there are certain sections of it which will cripple the fishing fleet of the Atlantic, and the coastal fleet especially.
There is in the bill a clause which defines steamers and steamships. Steamers and steamships include vessels propelled by auxiliary machinery. There are hundreds of fishing vessels equipped with auxiliary machinery and they will come under that provision, so that the coastal and fishing services will be affected. The result will be that every man who for the last ten, fifteen, twenty or thirty years has been able to command a vessel of that kind will be debarred from doing so. He must obtain a master's certificate ; he must have qualifications tantamount to the qualifications required to ensure the safety of ships carrying passengers. If that provision goes through as it stands, then you are crippling the fishing fleet on the Atlantic coast, and I do not know that you are not doing the same thing as regards the Pacific coast. I speak of the Atlantic coast because I am better acquainted with it and know the conditions that prevail there.
We should like to have an opportunity of consulting our people engaged in that industry before we as their representatives agree to the passage of this bill as it stands, and I think the bill would make greater progress if the minister would carry out the suggestion made by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough and defer its adoption. Let us have the second reading; I am not opposed to that, and I will not oppose the principle of the bill. But I am opposed and very strongly opposed to certain sections of it which in my opinion should be amended. But in trying to amend them I am not in a position to give to the house the information necessary to provide proper protection for the fishing fleet; I cannot give that information without having had an opportunity to consult those more directly interested in the fishing industry.
