interests of the fishermen and of the fishing industry have not been looked into with sufficient care in the preparation of the bill, so as to have the regulations of the Department of Fisheries conform with the bill, or to meet conditions, unavoidable in the past, which exist to-day and whereby fishermen entitled to bounties, owners of vessels, can be debarred from the enjoyment of those bounties owing to the fact that proper registration or proper transfer from one owner to another, in a great many instances, apparently has not been carried out.
Some provision should be made in this bill by which those entitled to bounty, those who find themselves in the position of having obtained the ownership of vessels under certain circumstances, shall have their interests safeguarded-for example, in cases of bankruptcy where, the liquidator not knowing the laws of Canada, liquidation has taken place through liquidators residing in England, representing companies established there one hundred years ago, with branches in Canada. These people established themselves in Canada along the Atlantic coast and, failing year by year, finally went into bankruptcy; but proper transfers were never made, so that the owners to-day do not know whether they legally own their vessels or not. They cannot obtain proper transfers from the liquidators, and there are hundreds of such cases.
If this bill had been as carefully looked into as it should have been, if the effect of registration had been compared with the regulations of the Fisheries department governing the payment of bounties, I am sure that some action would have been taken by the minister to meet the difficulty that exists to-day. It is an injustice to these fishermen; they are suffering more through the fault of the liquidators. If this aspect of the matter had been carefully investigated, I am sure that there would be in this bill some provision that would protect these people and entitle them to their regular bounties as if they were the original owners or held the original registration.
For these reasons I plead, with the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough, on behalf of the fishing industry on the Atlantic coast, that the adoption of this bill be deferred for a year in order to give to those interested in it an opportunity of studying the measure more carefully, so that we may be in a position to tell the house exactly what is necessary to protect the people engaged in this very hazardous industry.

As briefly and cogently as possible, I wish to identify myself with the suggestion made by the two hon. members who have preceded me. The Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) gave a very excellent introduction to the second reading of this measure. The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) and the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) have spoken in the interests of the industry on the Atlantic coast, and I wish to inform the minister that I have definite and specific representations from the shipping interests of the Pacific coast in opposition to many of the clauses of this bill. I do not think I will worry the house at the present time going into these representations in detail; I will reserve that for a future occasion. In a word or two however I wish to support the representations made by my two colleagues in impressing upon the minister the absolute necessity of deferring discussion in committee of the whole of this peculiar Anthony Adverse of legislative effort with which he has presented us at the eleventh hour of the session. This bill touches every shipping interest in the dominion on both the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts. If ever a measure came into the house deserving the earnest and sincere study of everyone who desires to advance the shipping industry of this country, we have it in this bulky legislation given to us only two days ago. If ever a special committee were required to study every single clause, phrase and paragraph, and ever possible implication and consequence of the various features of this measure, one is needed in regard to the legislation we have before us now. With all due respect, after a very strenuous session so far when we have given much consideration to minor pieces of legislation, it is unfair on the part of the government to ask the house in committee of the whole to discuss this measure just because it has received some study by a committee of another house. My information is that this bill after receiving such consideration was passed by another house practically in bulk without any study being given to the various clauses. In justice to constituents of mine who have important shipping interests in Vancouver, British Columbia, I suggest it is not fair to ask us to deal in committee of the whole with this measure at the present time practically at the eleventh [DOT] hour of the session and we should, as the minister says, pass the second reading, thus showing that we favour the principle of the bill, then pass one clause and at the next session of parliament appoint a committee on

Shipping Act-Mr. Cantley
shipping to go into every single phrase, paragraph and clause of this bill so that a measure may be produced that will be a monument to whatever parliament is in existence at that time.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) whether it is the intention to have this bill proclaimed this present year, or will it be subject to proclamation by the government later?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not in a position to answer that question, because obviously the answer lies with parliament itself as to what it may determine to do.

I presume the govern^
ment has some policy so far as that is concerned. I understood the object of introducing this bill this year was to provide a measure that might be discussed by the various dominions of the empire, witih the purpose eventually of producing legislation which would apply equally to all the dominions; this to be simply the nucleus of an act which the representatives of Canada could discuss with representatives of the other dominions.

And thus have uniformity
of legislation.

Whether that be so or not, I do not know, but I hope that is the situation. I agree with the two hon. members from the maritimes who have spoken in regard to some of the provisions of the bill. For instance, there is the matter of licensing masters of coasters. Fifty or sixty years ago, indeed, before and I think after confederation, a man who had served as mate and afterwards as captain for a series of years was given a certificate of servitude which enabled him to command our vessels on the high seas in any quarter of the globe. Some similar provision should be applied now so far as coasting and fishing vessels are concerned, whither sail or power propelled, of say less than three or four hundred tons. That, to my mind, is absolutely essential. I know men, and my two hon. friends opposite know more, who have commanded vessels for ten, fifteen or twenty years, men of forty or fifty years, of age who have had splendid records. If they are asked to pass an examination in regard to eyesight, a placard is put up fifteen or twenty feet away and they are requested to tell what the lettering on it is. They cannot without the aid of glasses do that, but they can see a ship half a mile or a mile and a half away at sea and say what flag she carries. Those are practical difficulties
that ought to be taken into consideration in any legislation of this kind, because they.are vital to the whole purpose of the bill.
If I understood the minister aright when he introduced the bill, he stated that it was the intention of the government to provide legislation which would control the shipping of Canada in all the ports of the world, or words to that effect. Might I remind the minister that before that can be effected it will be necessary for Canada to have consuls in all the great ports of the world. Those we have not got. We may talk as much as we please and as long as we like about being a nation, but until we have consuls in all or at least the principal ports of the world we are not able to exercise that sovereignty to which he referred. For instance, a Nova Scotia ship goes down to South America. She arrives at say the port of Rio de Janeiro. She has, we will say, three seamen in irons who have refused duty. What is she going to do with them? The captain wants them dealt with. He cannot on his own account put them into gaol in Rio de Janeiro. He has to apply to the British consul or to the British minister in that- port. It is idle to talk about our being a sovereign nation when we are in that position. Until we are in the position of a sovereign nation with our own consular officers in foreign ports he will not be able, nor will this government nor parliament be able, to do what the minister suggests, that is control, as he has suggested, our shipping in foreign waters. Those are matters which are vital and should be properly dealt with by this bill.	.
I have read a good many of the clauses. Some are all right; others objectionable, and, I have no doubt, will be amended or deleted before the bill passes the house. But, Mr. Speaker, I have not been very much exercised over this legislation by reason of the fact to which I have already referred, namely, that I presumed it was only a basis for discussion with the other component parts of the empire, and that as a result of that discussion a new measure would later be brought down to the house. If that view is correct I have nothing further to say in regard to the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks regarding this bill and join with the other speakers who have suggested that it had better be delayed for another year. I must first of all, like the others, compliment the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) on his presentation of this legislation. I was pleased
Shipping Act-Mr. Brown

to hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) suggest that perhaps it might be well to allow the bill to go into committee and then consider the advisability of postponing it for another year.
I might point out to the house that since the bill has been under discussion in the Senate I have received representations from many, including a captain who is also a port warden and w'ho has given this matter a great deal of consideration. So serious does he deem one of the clauses in this bill that he believes-and I agree with him-the measure should go to a committee of the house for discussion of this one clause alone, because he maintains that if clause 100 in the shape in which it has come from the Senate passes the house, it will add fifty per cent to the freight dues on all ships taking lumber from Vancouver or Prince Rupert or New Westminster or any other port in British Columbia. He says that it will also affect those ships in going through the Panama canal to Great Britain. Surely, if the information given to me is correct-I hold the brief in my hand; every phase of the matter has been gone into

that alone should make the government hesitate before attempting to have this bill pass through the house in committee of the whole.
Then questions are dealt with affecting seamen-seamen stranded on foreign shores, seamen in hospital, sick mariners' fund, the hiring and firing of seamen. I am in doubt as to whether the representatives of the seamen have been heard in these matters. When one looks over the various clauses affecting them and considers that the house is being asked to pass this bill in committee of the whole, I cannot but rise and protest. It would be wiser to have the bill referred to the committee of the whole house, perhaps at some other session.

It would be presumptuous for one like myself, who has lived most of his life half way between the Atlantic and the Pacific, to enter into a detailed discussion of this bill. There is however one section which affects those living on the prairies. The minister has referred to the fact that last year when the whole bill was withdrawn, a short bill was introduced, dealing with the protection of labour and with the coasting trade on the great lakes. That bill was passed, but my understanding was that it had never been proclaimed. The minister has stated that that bill is now the law of the land.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I said that the law, chapter 52 of the statutes of 1933, was incorporated in this bill.
Yes, but I understood the minister to say the bill we passed last year was now the law of the land.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: No.

Then I was right in my understanding that the bill has never been actually brought into force. It was really to find that out definitely that I rose.
Section 663 is the one that we prairie people are .particularly interested in, and if we give time to the bill in proportion to that given to some other legislation, as the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) suggested, I do not suppose we should reach that section until about the end of August. However, if it comes before the committee we shall be prepared to make recommendations.

Mr Speaker, I rise only to endorse briefly in general and very heartily the requests and suggestions of delay that have been made from this side of the house, especially the remarks of the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff), although I do not agree with him that it should be put into committee even at the present time, for reasons I shall give in a moment.
Turning aside for an instant to the remarks of the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot), he said there would be trouble in granting the bonus to the fishermen in the maritime provinces on account of the regulations in this bill in respect to registration. I hardly anticipate that would be as serious as he suggests, because if my recollection is right, and I am fairly certain it is, the act of 1882 providing for that bounty said that the money should be allocated according to regulations established by the Minister of Marine. Therefore if the existing regulations do not coincide with some registration features of this bill it would be easy to remake the regulations. That naturally suggests that the opportunity is overripe, when those regulations are being made, to undo a wrong that has been done to British Columbia for many years and make provision for our fishermen on the Pacific coast to share in that bounty the same as the Atlantic men. They are absolutely entitled to it by the law of the land, and they have been unjustly deprived by the malformation, so to speak, of these regulations. I shall not detain the house longer on that matter, because it is too

Shipping Act-Mr. Neill
obvious and the necessity for it too crying to require elaboration.
I do not think we should pass the second reading of this bill unless we have the positive assurance that it will go no further this year. I accept the ever present cordiality of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) and we recognize his integrity, but he did not make a definite promise. If he had I would have been satisfied, but I recall that some weeks ago we thought we had reason to believe- perhaps we were deceiving ourselves-that we would succeed in the agitation we were making to have the marketing bill sent to a select committee. But there was a little noise and confusion one day and we found a motion was put to go into committee and when we were in committee of the whole and began to protest we were told plainly that we had lost our opportunity, the bill was in committee and was going to stay there; and stay there it did, with an enormous waste of time that we would be very sorry to see duplicated in respect of this bill.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) said that he had received many objections from the Pacific coast. I think objections would be much more numerous if people concerned really knew what the bill means, but as no one knows what it means, of course it is impossible for them to make very urgent objections. Among others I am only going to quote one, just to give an idea of the futility of men even as well informed as we are supposed to be, dealing with this matter in committee of the whole and not being able to have technical advisers, as we could in select committee. Here is one request I have received. These people say:
We request that the present method of computing the nominal horse power of propelling engines be discontinued, and brake or shaft horse power be substituted for all turbine and internal combustion engines, and indicated horse power for all reciprocating steam engines.
How many men are there in this house who really know what that means, let alone are able to pass an intelligent opinion as to how it should be brought about? Certainly I am not.
Another aspect of the matter is this: are we to pass this legislation or is it to be passed in a place that I must leave nameless? After all I think the House of Commons is responsible for passing legislation. The minister says it is very complete, that they have studied it for years. But we remember a former bill that was studied at great length in another place, and no doubt they gave it much care and attention-the bill con' 74726-242
nected with the amalgamation of railways. When it was brought here the same eulogistic remarks were made, that we did not need to do much more than sign our names because it had been so thoroughly considered by these able elder statesmen, but when the bill finally passed this house its own mother would not have known it, so different was it from when it left the other chamber. So we must not take it for granted that because it has been seriously and earnestly considered in another place it is going to receive unanimous support in this house. It is all very well to pass divorce bills and matters of that kind; we can afford to take a chance on that, but these are serious things.
Then the minister says that it was open to any of us who were interested to go to the other place. Well, that sounds reasonable, but it is not so reasonable as it sounds. In the first place we have about enough to do attending committees of this house; are we to undertake the duty of attending senate committees? Another thing, we have not facilities for knowing when those committees meet. And I do not know that we would be particularly welcome if we went there and butted into their deliberations, as the expression is. If we wished to give evidence we would be graciously received, but as far as taking part in the committee is concerned, I would not ask it for one thing; it is their committee and it would not be for us to go there and express opinions and take part in the voting.
Then again we are told that there have been important changes made by the committee and subcommittee in another house. What were those changes? No one is able to tell us I sent to another chamber this afternoon and asked for the copy of the committee proceedings, where all the serious consideration had been given, in order that I might inform myself. I wanted to know who these various people are that we are told about, from everywhere except British Columbia apparently, who gave such voluminous evidence. The answer I received was that the evidence taken before the Senate committee, that committee of another place, had not been printed and therefore was not accessible to me. I do not know what took place. I do not know what arguments were used; they may have been good or they may have been bad. They may have been ex parte arguments. The witnesses are gone-I do not know where. I have no means of getting that information. I simply have to take the minister's word that a number of worthy people gave evidence, but we do not know any more than does the man in



Shipping Act-Mr. Hanbury
the moon what evidence they gave. We can only guess as to what happened by looking at the bill now before us and comparing it with what was introduced in the Senate. Is that a desirable condition, and are we to be guided simply by that? I know that every man who rises in his place in this committee and finds fault with a section will be told that it was carefully considered in another place, a place where they had all the advantages of hearing witnesses, and that we must be satisfied. I will not accept that doctrine as a guide in the consideration of this bill. I want to know at least something about what we are doing. Hon. members who have spoken have indicated the time it would take to carry this bill through committee of the whole this session if it is given anything like proper consideration. It is impossible at this time in the session to have the bill placed before the committee on marine and fisheries; it is too late to get witnesses. Let it pass second reading, if we must. Then let us take the bill home, where people will be able to give us advice. Then early next session let us send it to the marine and fisheries committee, instead of trying to do anything more with it at this time.
I have a note before me which indicates that some people living at remote distances sent written recommendations to the committee which sat in another place. We have not those communications, and will not be able to have them on the floor of the house. If we had the services of technical men before the marine committee we could handle the bill very much more quickly, but it is far too late to do that now, and if that procedure is not followed a gross injustice will be perpetrated. I am merely duplicating the remarks which have been better expressed by other hon. members, but I could sum up what I have said by stating simply that any further procedure at this time would amount to a serious injustice. There are features in this bill the meaning of which is not clear; we may find out after it is too late, and there would be a howl go up which would bring us into disgrace.
The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) asked if the bill was going to be brought into effect this year. There is a section of the bill-and I happened to glance at it when I was browsing through it- stipulating that the government may bring the whole bill into effect when and if they like, or they may bring any part of it into effect. Well now, a reaction which would be extremely undesirable may arise in that connection. One part may

be brought in which would conflict with something else. As the hon. member for Pictou has indicated, a steamer may reach South America and then find that a particular section under which it is operating has been brought into effect, and some other section of equal moment has not been brought into effect. I decline absolutely to accept the approval of any other body, nor am I willing to take any responsibility for the passing of this bill, if in the present session it is jammed through this House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, before the minister replies I should like to take only one moment to add my support to the respresentations made by the various members who have suggested that this legislation should be held over until next year. While it is true, or at least altogether likely, that much consideration has been given to the drafting of the bill, and that it has been very carefully studied by the committee in another place, still I think it is unfair for the government at this time to expect hon. members to accept legislation of this type and magnitude, really a whole library of legislation, without taking time to give it consideration. The government should tell the house that it wants hon. members to go through this measure clause by clause, to give it the consideration which the people of Canada expect hon. members to give to legislation handed down from another place, and to ascertain whether it is properly or improperly drafted. I make a very strong representation to the government in support of hon. members who have already said that in fairness to this House of Commons and in fairness to our sense of responsibility to our constituents and to the people of Canada as a whole we should not be asked to attach our names to this measure in the present session, if we hope to get home before Christmas.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to associate myself with the former speakers, and state that this legislation is too bulky and brought down too late in the session to receive action from this chamber. I have received several representations from fishermen and shipping interests on the Pacific coast saying that they would like to have copies of the bill so that they may study it and make themselves available to give information affecting the Pacific coast. I understand that the present measure is based on British legislation passed a number of years ago, in days when there were different marine

Shipping Act-Mr. Duranleau
methods, and before the development of diesel and gas engines. Developments in late years have been so great it is quite possible that this measure based on legislation passed years ago would not suit present day needs.
I strongly urge that this matter be referred to a committee to sit at the next session, so that they may be in a position to obtain the necessary information applying to modern shipping.

Mr. Speaker, from this corner of the house I wish to say exactly the same as other hon. members have been saying. This is not a bill, it is an encyclopaedia, and if we give proportionately as much time to its consideration as we did to consideration of the marketing bill we will be here until next session, and probably the session after that. And if a constitutional problem should happen to crop up in the present measure we may be still longer. I think sound advice has been given to the government. I have received a number of representations from organizations on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts concerning features in this bill to which certain interests are strenuously opposed. Then, there are other sections in the bill which vitally affect the welfare of the people on the prairies who ship via the great lakes. Certainly the government would be well advised if they accepted the advice of hon. members on this side of the house and committed the bill to a committee to sit next session-of course assuming that the government will be here next year.
It will be.
I think so myself; however, I shall not discuss that point.
You and I know, anyway.

If the matter were
placed before a committee those who understand shipping and its technical ramifications could appear and give advice concerning the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I understand the bill now before the house has not been submitted to the provinces for their consideration. Bearing in mind the fact that the province of Quebec has full charge of its fisheries, and the further fact that the pilot services for the lower St. Lawrence as well as the upper St. Lawrence are materially affected in this new bill, I wish to the best of my ability to support the 71726-2425
representations which have been made by hon. members who have preceded me in this debate. I believe it would be quite unfair to consider this bill at the present session, first because the province of Quebec has not had a chance to peruse it and, secondly, because hon. members of this house have not had a chance to study it clause by clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I say that the same difficulty arose in another house. When the bill was reported and before it had been read by hon. members the same objections were made. But after two days had elapsed and hon. members had read the bill they came to the conclusion it was not so complicated, and with perhaps slight amendment could be adopted, and it was. I am prepared to accept the suggestion made by my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), because every hon. member accepts the principle of the bill. I am willing to proceed to committee of the whole and have the first clause adopted, and then move that the committee rise.
That is all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I refer to the title, The Canada Shipping Act, 1934.
And what then?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: If no hon. member has any objection to the title, we may pass that clause and then I would move that the committee rise. But in the meantime I would invite my hon. friends to take this volume home with them-
It is a library.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: -and to pass their week-end studying it. It is not so complicated after all.
Have mercy upon us, Mr. Minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
There are perhaps not more than twenty-five clauses on which discussion would take place in committee of the whole. There are, for instance, some clauses about pilotage, some about the size and measurement of ships, decks, and so on, but surely there will be no objection to eighty per cent of the clauses of the bill, which is in part a reproduction of the merchant shipping acts which are the result of centuries of experience in England and the British Empire. The provisions that were adopted by various international conferences, the load line convention and the convention for safety of life at sea,
Canada Shipping Act

have been reproduced in this bill, and those provisions are very voluminous. These conventions were adhered to by Canada and practically all the countries of the world, and we had to embody them in this bill. I am sure that when my hon. friends have devoted a few hours to a study of the bill-
It will take a week.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: No. I held the same view when the bill came to me, but if my hon. friend from Rimouski will take the trouble to spend a few hours on the bill I think he will come to the conclusion that it should be considered in committee of the whole house and be adopted at this session.

It will
take a week to read it.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
As was stated a few
moments ago by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley), if we pass the bill this session it will be an inducement to all the other parts of the empire to adopt similar legislation. When I hear some hon. gentlemen say that this bill is not an urgent one, I desire to recall that ever since I became Minister of Marine in 1930 I have had queries from the other side of the house at every session, even at the first short session in September 1930, asking when a full revision of the Canada Shipping Act was to be brought down. Those queries were repeated at every session, and I gathered from that, that everybody was anxious that this law should be enacted in the interests of Canada. I invite my hon. friends to peruse the bill over the week-end, and then I am sure they will come back next week with an entirely different opinion. I assure my hon. friends that if we go on with the bill this session every opportunity will be given to every member to discuss every clause of the bill if that is desired, but I do not think it will be necessary.

If the minister wants us
to read this bill over the week-end what shall we do on Sunday without church?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
You can go to mass
in the morning and then start reading.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Smith (Cumberland) in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

I know it is not the desire of the committee to raise any controversy tonight, but there is one question which I think the minister might well answer. In the bill of last year, letter J of the Senate, there were

821 sections, and in this new bill there are 719 sections, or 102 sections fewer. Would the minister be good enough to explain just what happened? Was there an amalgamation of some sections?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I think that a great number of the sections of the bill J of last year have been embodied in other sections of this bill as subsections. My hon. friend will notice that a great number of the sections cover one or two pages, and contain five or six or seven subsections. That is the reason for the sections being fewer in this bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the section carry?

I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that if we let this section through we are sunk; we are committed to putting the whole bill through. The minister was very pleasant in his manner of explaining things, but the real iron hand beneath the silken glove was evident. He does intend to go on with this bill, and he told the Scotchmen to read it on the sabbath day, more shame to him! He said he would adopt the suggestion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) but the Minister of Finance did not go any further than to suggest adjourning the discussion and then considering the situation. If he is going to consider it, why not do the considering now? We all know that this section is the only one on which we can have any general discussion. Once we pass this, we can be held by the rules to a definite and particular section, and we cannot go beyond the scope of that particular section. In that way we shall be compelled to go right through the bill. The minister has not made any promise that he will do anything else. I think we would be ill advised, considering the experience we have had with other matters, if we passed even this first section unless we can get a clear understanding along the lines suggested. If the minister is not able to say anything definite before consulting with his colleagues, let us adjourn now. It is quite sufficient to go into committee and then report progress. That keeps the procedure proper, and then the minister can discuss the situation with his colleagues and announce his intention when the bill comes before us again. But we should not pass this first section, which would preclude us from any general discussion, without knowing where we get off at.

There is something in what
my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) says. I would suggest that clause 1 stand, and that we take up clause 2, and pass

the first subsection of it. I mention that because of the closeness of the definition to my own title. Subsection 1 reads:
"The Admiralty" means the Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom for the time being, or the commissioners for the time being for executing the office of Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom.
We can pass that.

The minister stated that there had been a demand for this legislation, and he based his statement upon the many inquiries he had received from the members of the house during the past three or four years as to when this bill was to be brought down.

been demanded not only in this house, but has been requested by shipping interests all over the country.

The house resumed from Monday, June 4, consideration in committee of Bill No. 89, to amend and consolidate the Excise Act-Mr. Matthews-Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton South) in the chair.
On section 124-Penalties belong to crown.

When this bill was in committee a few days ago all the sections were passed with the exception of some in which it was suggested that the governor in council should be substituted for the minister. I think this suggestion was made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and in conformity with it I have prepared amendments covering sections 124, 126, 127, 155, 156, 159, 161, 180, 216, 235, 236 and 262. I shall ask my colleague, the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) to move the amendment in connection with this section.

I move:
That subsection 1 of section 124 of the bill to amend and consolidate the Excise Act be struck out and the following substituted therefor:-
124 (1). All penalties and forfeitures under this act shall belong to His Majesty for the public uses of Canada.
Provided that-
(a)	the proceeds of any such penalties and forfeitures may, under such regulations as the governor in council may from time to time prescribe in that behalf, be distributed' in whole or in part and may be divided between and paid to any officer and any person giving information or otherwise aiding in effecting a seizure resulting in any such penalty or forfeiture;
(b)	the governor in council may by such regulations prescribe the manner in which the proceeds of penalties and forfeitures shall be distributed and may provide for payment of awards forthwith after seizure of goods or the preferring of charges where goods are not seized, based upon the value of the goods seized, the amount of excise duty evaded, the penalties imposable upon any person guilty of any violation of this act, as the case may be, and not dependent upon forfeiture or the proceeds of forfeiture.
I should like to ask the minister how this change compares with the law as it is now.

This section corresponds to section 133 of the existing act which has been rewritten to bring the excise act into line with the practice long ago adopted under the Customs Act of paying for information received if such information results in conviction and the imposition of penalties even though the net proceeds may be a loss. That is, the fine is not paid; the convicted person may prefer to serve time, or the necessary expenses may exceed the amount realized.

Do I understand from the
minister that this is to make this section the same as the section in the Customs Act?
Excise Act
Yes, it makes it conform to the section in that act.

I realize
that this provision is in the statutes, but it seems to me to be a vicious principle to give a portion of the fine to an official under salary and permanently employed for the purpose of detecting evasions of the customs or excise acts. I can understand that an outside informer who assists in obtaining a conviction might be entitled to some portion of the fine, but I cannot understand why an individual who is paid for that job-

Not always.
Mr .STEWART (Edmonton): Not always. As it now stands a permanent salaried officer will be entitled to a portion of the fine if he secures a conviction. I am just asking the minister if he is considering this matter.

That matter has
received very careful consideration. Ever since 1867 the Customs Act has contained a similar clause in connection with moieties, and it is now being placed in this bill. It will be noted that the section as it now reads confers the power on the governor in council-
Mr .STEWART (Edmonton): That is not the point; my point is the principle of paying a portion of the fine to a paid official of the department.

It must be remembered that the governor in council can decide at any time whether a moiety shall be paid. At the present time I think it would be better to pass this clause in order to have it in conformity with the Customs Act which has been in force so long. If I may say so, I believe this whole question of moiety payments may receive consideration before the Customs Act is amended and consolidated, which may happen within a measurable time.

In my time I have been an officer in the customs and excise, and when it is said that an officer receiving salary on full time should not receive any consideration in the matter of seizures, I think that is going a little too far. An officer on full time in the customs and excise, during the time I was in the service, received his salary and his hours were defined

nine o'clock in the morning until four in the afternoon. Those were the hours for which he was paid. Very frequently in those days seizures were made at all hours during the twenty-four, and they were made principally at night. I served for eleven years in the customs and excise, and in those days a

customs officer had to do inland revenue service-excise service-without pay. He received pay for his service as collector of customs and then if he did work after hours for the excise and inland he received a certain small -commission that hardly compensated him for the time he put in. Having had considerable experience in matters of seizure, I say this to the committee. You are doing right when you provide that an officer who is zealous in carrying out his duties should receive a part of th'e fine. When I was in the service, an officer who made any seizure did not undertake a task as hazardous as the task that is now involved. Many times in the last few years, in the last eight or ten years, an officer to carry out what he deemed- to be his duty had to risk his life, and he is to-day doing so. Perhaps members of the committee have no idea of what a seizing officer who wishes to be zealous in the discharge of his duty is up against when he comes across smugglers and hi-jaekers. Those who have had experience in that line as I have had will feel it an injustice, I am sure, to cut off the extra remuneration, because, to-day more than at any time in my experience, the officer is risking his life every twenty-four hours he is after smugglers.

With regard to the moiety system I must admit that I was never particularly convinced of the propriety of it, although it -has its qualifications as outlined by the ex-Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot). I should think that the minister might very well reconsider the whole question, and possibly it might be arranged on a somewhat different basis, though I have no particular suggestion to offer at the moment. I think he is right when he desires to put the administration of the act, so far as moieties are concerned, on the same basis as the Customs Act. I think also that it is time the Customs Act was revised, and when that is done the two acts, the excise act and the act that is being revised now, should be brought entirely into conformity.
With regard to the moiety system I want to ask the minister this question. I believe that in the customs preventive service, now in the hands of the mounted police, -the system of distributing moieties has been changed; instead of the individual receiving the moiety, I understand that the amount is paid into a central fund and then distributed among the various officers of the force whether or not they had any part in the particular seizure. Can the minister explain more in detail just how that is working out, and whether it makes

Excise Act
for better service and satisfaction among the members of the force?
Another question. In my recollection, which is none too good, eases would come up where an officer would make a seizure of what would ordinarily be a very valuable cargo of alcohol or whisky or some other liquor, and under the regulations of the department this valuable commodity would be destroyed, and there would be nothing on which to base the value of the moiety. Is there any change in that regard? I always felt at that time that, when a person had made the seizure-it might not have been the officer at all but a layman assisting in making the seizure-and a valuable cargo of liquor had been destroyed under the regulations of the department, there being in consequence no value on which to base the moiety, there should be some means of compensating the man who had made the seizure for the work he had done.

As to the first question, there is a central fund and the amount at the end of the year is distributed among the officers. As regards the second question, where there is no real value in the goods seized, authority is given to make an allowance up to S500.

This new arrangement of
distribution applies to both excise and customs?
Yes.

Now that the question of
moieties has been brought up, I think it would be well to consider the position of municipalities in this connection. In the municipality I reside in, very often it is the municipal police who make both seizure and charge, and I think it is a little unfair that no part of the fine should go to the municipality. Instead, part of it goes to the informer and part to the dominion government, and where there is imprisonment for a term of less than two years the province and the municipality have to pay for the prisoner's upkeep in gaol. Of course, if it is over two years, he goes to the penitentiary under federal jurisdiction. I think it wrould be well to consider the position of municipalities, such as there are in British Columbia, whose officers make and have made seizures, but the fines in connection with which go to the federal government, *while the cost of policing is borne entirely by the municipality. Rather than have the whole of the moiety go to the officer, I think part of it should go to the municipality that is responsible for policing and seizure.
I do not remember whether there is any provision in the Customs Act whereby the department has paid for the upkeep of a prisoner during the period of his incarceration.

There is no such
provision.

Well, the federal government does not go as far as provincial governments do in carrying out provincial liquor acts. Where a person is convicted for violating the provincial liquor law and confined to the county gaol, they make arrangements with the municipality to pay the board, so to spgak, of the individual so incarcerated. I have often thought lately whether it was fair for the dominion government to make an arrest for a violation of the customs or the excise act, to confine the person convicted to prison for a period running, say from three to fifteen months, and to allow the municipality to pay the expenses of the upkeep of that individual in gaol. In order to relieve the municipalities to a certain extent, especially during these hard times, we ought to make some provision whereby in the case of a person convicted under this or the customs act and imprisoned, the department concerned of the federal government should at least look after the expense of that individual to the county while he is in the county gaol. Will the minister take that into consideration?
Certainly.

I think this question of
paying a moiety to the informer is really embodying a very vicious system in this measure that is being put through. Of course the provision has always been there, but it is absolutely unfair for the government to be a party to paying a moiety of a fine to an informer who possibly just out of ill will to his neighbour informs on him in respect of some minor offence. The man is put in gaol and his family left, as has been stated, to the mercy of the community to be taken care of. That is really encouraging a system which to my mind should not be tolerated, especially when an officer is paid a handsome salary for doing his duty. If under such conditions he cannot conscientiously give time to his position without being a partaker of the fine which the poor chap has to pay, such an officer is not worthy of being an official.
Poor chap?

I am not so much concerned with those who make this a matter of business as with the maker of home brew,
Excise Act

who is usually a poor man. These people do this because very often they have no other way of getting a few cents together; frequently they are not able to pay their fine unless somebody comes to their assistance; They are put in gaol and their families left to be taken care of, in Prince Edward Island, by the province, because we have no municipal councils or districts. The minister should give us a statement of the amount of money distributed yearly in moieties.

I am informed that
last year the distribution to officers was about $4,900 for the whole of Canada.

Does that include all the
moieties to the officers and informers? The officer making the seizure under information given by an informer is not allowed to give the name of the informer to the department, the department does not exact it from him.

That is the amount
paid to the officers.

That it has been an unqualified success in past years has been due to the fact that it had the devoted and assiduous attention of the representatives of the fourth estate who are associated with us in parliament, and so that it may have the same success to-morrow night as in previous years I hope that the representatives of the fourth estate will have the opportunity through an early adjournment to-night of addressing themselves solely to its well being. In fact this event is of such importance as to transcend all other considerations not excepting the business of the high court of parliament itself. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move that the house do now adjourn.
Before we adjourn I suggest to the minister that it would be a happy thought to allow us to adjourn so that members of the house may rest as well.

Before the question is put I would like to take this opportunity of directing the attention of the Minister of

Finance and the government to the fact that some of us come from places many hundreds and indeed thousands of miles away. We have been here now for four and a half months, and we are hoping to get home. I trust the government will take into consideration Wednesday evening sittings or morning sittings as soon as possible. When time may be taken to encourage the members of the fourth estate and to celebrate Empire day and things of that sort, I hope we shall be given some consideration by the session being brought to a close so that hon. members may be permitted to get back to their homes and business.
